title: Useful AI Resources and Tools
author: IntelligentDot2924
selftext:
Claude and GPT aren’t the only options for AI-assisted game development. Different models and tools can help with planning, coding, art, and local experimentation, and you can combine them instead of relying on one provider for everything.



**Model providers**

**Ollama Cloud** provides hosted access to open models through Ollama. It gives you another option for coding help, debugging, documentation, and brainstorming without running a model on your own hardware. Ollama also supports local models.

**OpenCode Go** is a subscription that provides access to coding models for use with OpenCode. It’s an alternative to relying only on Claude or GPT subscriptions, with access to models from providers such as DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, and others. Available models and usage limits may change.

**OpenRouter** provides a single API for models from many providers. You can compare models on the same task, choose based on cost or speed, and switch models without setting up each provider’s API separately. 

[**Fal.ai**](http://Fal.ai) hosts models for generating images, video, audio, and 3D assets. In game development, these can help with concept art, textures, animation references, or quick asset prototypes. Generated assets may still need editing and optimization before production use. 



**Tools and local options**

**OpenCode** is an open-source coding agent, or harness, that connects models to your codebase and tools. It can inspect and edit files, run commands and tests, and work through longer tasks. Unlike a tool tied to one model provider, it can connect to models from many providers, including local models. 

Its workflow is more configurable than simply chatting with Claude or GPT. OpenCode sessions persist so you can close the terminal and resume later. It supports MCP tools, which let you connect the agent to external tools and services. You can also use different models for Plan and Build: for example, have Claude, GPT or GLM reason through the task and make a plan, then have DeepSeek or Mercury implement it. DeepSeek through Ollama Cloud can generate around **260 tokens per second**, while Mercury 2.5 through Inception can reach around 1**,107 tokens per second** (It's a diffusion text model.). That means you can reserve a strong reasoning model for planning and use a much faster model for implementation and text-heavy work. Those speeds depend on the specific provider **DeepSeek with Ollama** and **Mercury with Inception**, but they illustrate why separating the models can cut waiting time substantially.

OpenCode doesn’t make a model inherently smarter, and there isn’t one universal benchmark proving it always outperforms Codex or Claude Code. Its strength is the flexibility to choose models, connect tools, configure agents, and continue work across sessions. The model still determines much of the reasoning and code quality, and generated code needs review and testing.

As of October 11, 2026, the latest listed v1 release is **v1.19.0**, with OpenCode 2 also available as a separate upgrade path. Check the release channel when installing so you know which version you’re using. I personally recommend V2 as the QoL is massive. With the right setup you can straight up make the coding portion autonomous I still recommend having some basic understanding of what you are doing and do rigorous testing.

**Strata** runs the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model locally on compatible gaming PCs with NVIDIA or AMD graphics. It’s designed to run a large model by spreading work across GPU memory and system RAM, and it exposes APIs that coding agents can use. That makes it an option for experimenting with a powerful local model rather than sending every request to a cloud service. Hardware and RAM requirements are significant, so check whether your PC is supported. 16GB GPU and 64GB of System RAM DDR4/5 recommended.

**Diffusion models** generate images from text prompts or reference images. They can help with concept art, textures, and visual exploration. **ComfyUI** lets you build image-generation workflows, including local ones. Larger models need more GPU memory, so local performance depends on your hardware.



**Other useful projects**

**Reverse Engineer Anything (REA)** by morluto helps an AI agent inspect applications and binaries. It can be useful for exploring how existing software behaves or understanding unfamiliar systems.

**Skills For Real Engineers** by Matt Pocock provides reusable instructions for coding agents, helping them follow structured engineering practices when working on a project.

**Agent Skills** by Addy Osmani is a collection of capabilities and instructions that can extend compatible agents with task-specific workflows.

**Diagram Design** by Cathryn Lavery helps coding agents create diagrams, which can be useful for explaining game architecture, gameplay systems, or data flow.

**Knowledge-Work-Plugins** by Anthropic provides plugins for common knowledge-work workflows. It isn’t specifically game-focused, but may help with documentation and project organization.

**Open Code Review** by Alibaba focuses on AI-assisted code review. It can help check changes to gameplay code, tools, or other project systems.

**LiteLLM** by BerriAI provides a common interface for connecting to and routing requests across model providers, making it easier to experiment with multiple models in one project.

There are also Jev models, but that is a bit advanced and not really useful unless you have a crazy setup like PewDiePie.
